title: Identifying a diode, an LED, a resistor and a capacitor
objective: To examine a mixed collection of electronic components and identify each one.
To use an ohmmeter in both directions as the test that distinguishes them.
To justify each identification from the evidence rather than from appearance.

theory.statement: Four kinds of component in a school kit can be told apart by what an ohmmeter does when its probes are reversed. A resistor has no polarity, so it reads the same both ways. A diode is a p-n junction: it conducts when forward-biased and blocks when reverse-biased, so it reads low one way and open the other. An LED is also a junction, but its forward voltage is about 1.8 V rather than 0.7 V, so its forward reading is markedly higher. A capacitor blocks steady current in both directions, but while it charges from the meter’s internal cell the needle kicks and then falls back.
keyEquations: A resistor reads the same resistance whichever way round the probes go.
A junction conducts one way only — that asymmetry is what identifies a diode or an LED.
An LED’s forward reading is much higher than a diode’s, because its junction needs more voltage.
A capacitor reads open in the steady state, but the initial kick separates it from a break.
Appearance is not evidence: several components in the tray look like each other.

apparatus.name: Mixed tray of components
apparatus.why: The specimens to be identified; several are deliberately ambiguous to look at.

apparatus.name: Digital multimeter on the ohms range
apparatus.why: Supplies a small current from its own cell, so the component can be tested out of circuit.

apparatus.name: Crocodile-clip leads
apparatus.why: Hold the component so both hands are free and the probes do not slip.

procedure: Take a specimen from the tray and look at its body. Note the shape, any bands and any printed code.
Clip it to the meter on the ohms range and read the resistance.
Reverse the connections and read it again. This second reading is the one that matters.
If the needle kicks and falls back, watch it carefully — that is a capacitor charging.
Decide what the component is, using both readings and not the appearance alone.
Record the identification and repeat until all four kinds have been found.

steps: Compare the two ohmmeter readings for each specimen.
Equal and finite both ways → resistor.
Low one way, open the other → a junction: diode if the forward reading is low, LED if it is high.
Open both ways with an initial kick → capacitor.

expectedResult.statement: All four kinds can be identified from the ohmmeter readings alone. The resistors read the same both ways; the diodes and LEDs read one way only; the capacitors read open both ways. The two junction devices are separated by the size of the forward reading, which reflects a forward voltage of about 0.7 V for silicon against about 1.8 V for a light-emitting junction.

safety: Test components out of circuit only. An ohmmeter applied to a live circuit gives a meaningless reading and may damage the meter.
Discharge any large capacitor before handling it; a charged capacitor can hold a painful voltage.
Do not force component legs into the clips — repeated bending snaps them.
sourcesOfError: Judging by appearance instead of testing: several specimens look like each other.
Testing in one direction only, which cannot distinguish a junction from a resistor.
Missing the brief kick of a small capacitor and calling it a broken component.
Touching both probes with the fingers, so body resistance appears in parallel with the component.
Expecting an LED to light on the ohms range; usually there is too little current.

viva.question: Which single test separates a resistor from a diode?
viva.expectedConcept: Reversing the probes: a resistor reads the same both ways, a diode does not.
viva.answerLogic: Reversing the probes: a resistor reads the same both ways, a diode does not.
viva.commonMisconception: That the reading in one direction is enough.

viva.question: Both a diode and an LED conduct one way only. How do you tell them apart with an ohmmeter?
viva.expectedConcept: The forward reading is much higher for an LED, because its junction needs about 1.8 V rather than 0.7 V.
viva.answerLogic: The forward reading is much higher for an LED, because its junction needs about 1.8 V rather than 0.7 V.
viva.commonMisconception: That an LED must light up to be recognised.

viva.question: A specimen reads open circuit both ways. What could it be?
viva.expectedConcept: A capacitor, or a broken component. The initial kick as it charges distinguishes them.
viva.answerLogic: A capacitor, or a broken component. The initial kick as it charges distinguishes them.
viva.commonMisconception: That open circuit always means faulty.

viva.question: Why does a capacitor show a kick and then fall back to open?
viva.expectedConcept: The meter’s cell charges the capacitor; current flows only while the charge builds, then stops.
viva.answerLogic: The meter’s cell charges the capacitor; current flows only while the charge builds, then stops.
viva.commonMisconception: That a capacitor conducts steadily at DC.

viva.question: Why is a small ceramic capacitor harder to identify than an electrolytic one?
viva.expectedConcept: Its capacitance is far smaller, so it charges almost instantly and the kick is too brief to see.
viva.answerLogic: Its capacitance is far smaller, so it charges almost instantly and the kick is too brief to see.
viva.commonMisconception: That all capacitors behave identically on test.

viva.question: What does the marking 104 on a small disc mean?
viva.expectedConcept: 10 followed by four zeros picofarad, that is 100 nF.
viva.answerLogic: 10 followed by four zeros picofarad, that is 100 nF.
viva.commonMisconception: That it is a serial number or a resistance code.

viva.question: Why must components be tested out of circuit?
viva.expectedConcept: Other components in parallel provide alternative paths, so the reading is not that of the component alone.
viva.answerLogic: Other components in parallel provide alternative paths, so the reading is not that of the component alone.
viva.commonMisconception: That an ohmmeter always reads the component it touches.

viva.question: What physical difference gives an LED its higher forward voltage?
viva.expectedConcept: A wider band gap, chosen so that the recombination energy is emitted as visible light.
viva.answerLogic: A wider band gap, chosen so that the recombination energy is emitted as visible light.
viva.commonMisconception: That the colour comes from the plastic lens.

viva.question: A student identifies a component as a resistor after one reading of 470 Ω. What is missing?
viva.expectedConcept: The reverse reading. A forward-biased diode could also read a few hundred ohms.
viva.answerLogic: The reverse reading. A forward-biased diode could also read a few hundred ohms.
viva.commonMisconception: That a plausible resistance value proves it is a resistor.

viva.question: How can you tell which leg of an LED is the anode without a meter?
viva.expectedConcept: The longer leg is the anode; the flat on the rim marks the cathode.
viva.answerLogic: The longer leg is the anode; the flat on the rim marks the cathode.

preLab.question: Which property of a p-n junction makes it identifiable with an ohmmeter?
options: It conducts in one direction only
preLab.feedback: A p-n junction is the only thing in the tray that conducts one way and blocks the other.

preLab.question: A resistor connected the other way round reads:
preLab.feedback: A resistor has no polarity, so reversing the probes changes nothing.

duringLab.question: Test each specimen in BOTH directions before naming it.
Identify at least four different specimens from the tray.

postLab.question: Why is the forward reading of an LED higher than that of a silicon diode?
options: Its junction needs a larger forward voltage
It has more resistance in its leads
postLab.feedback: A wider band gap means a larger forward drop, and the light that comes with it.

postLab.question: The safest way to identify an unmarked component is to:
options: Assume it matches the others in the tray
postLab.feedback: One reading cannot distinguish a resistor from a forward-biased junction.
